claims.text: An optimal intermediate level of atomic disorder enhances superconductivity in high-entropy alloys.
Intermediate atomic disorder maximizes electron-phonon coupling needed for Cooper-pair formation.
Greater atomic order than the optimum reduces the superconducting transition temperature.
Excessive atomic disorder reduces the superconducting transition temperature.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase solid-solution HEA containing at least five elements, each at 5 atomic percent or more.
The as-synthesized starting material has a nominally moderate level of atomic disorder.
Changing elemental ratios can systematically tune atomic disorder while leaving overall electron density approximately constant.
The relevant structural mediator is short-range atomic order or disorder expressed through variations in local atomic environments.
Moderate chemical disorder increases scattering events that enhance electron-phonon interactions and favor pairing.
Moderate disorder can enhance pairing without localizing charge carriers.
Too little disorder fails to activate pairing-favorable scattering pathways sufficiently.
Excessive disorder disrupts electron coherence and thereby lowers the superconducting transition temperature.
Samples engineered to have intermediate disorder will have a higher transition temperature than the as-synthesized baseline.
Samples with reduced disorder will have a lower transition temperature than the baseline.
Samples with excessive disorder will have a lower transition temperature than the baseline.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions and each element remains at or above 5 atomic percent.
The proposed relationship is not expected to apply when compositions cause phase separation or substantial changes in overall electron density.
The disorder–transition-temperature relationship and the optimal disorder level may depend on the specific elemental combination.
